In [[spatial ecology]] and [[macroecology]], '''scaling pattern of occupancy''' ('''SPO'''), also known as the '''area-of-occupancy''' ('''AOO''') is the way in which species distribution changes across spatial scales.  In [[physical geography]] and [[image analysis]], it is similar to the [[modifiable areal unit problem]]. [[Simon A. Levin]] (1992)<ref>Levin, SA. 1992. The problem of pattern and scale in ecology. Ecology, 73, 1943–1967.[http://www.esajournals.org/doi/abs/10.2307/1941447]</ref> states that ''the problem of relating phenomena across scales is the central problem in biology and in all of science''. Understanding the SPO is thus one central theme in ecology.

== Pattern description ==

This pattern is often plotted as log-transformed grain (cell size) versus log-transformed occupancy. Kunin (1998)<ref>Kunin, WE. 1998. Extrapolating species abundance across spatial scales. Science, 281: 1513–1515.[http://www.sciencemag.org/cgi/content/full/281/5382/1513]</ref> presented a log-log linear SPO and suggested a fractal nature for species distributions. It has since been shown to follow a [[Logistic distribution|logistic]] shape, reflecting a [[percolation]] process. Furthermore, the SPO is closely related to the intraspecific [[occupancy-abundance relationship]]. For instance, if individuals are randomly distributed in space, the number of individuals in an ''α''-size cell follows a [[Poisson distribution]], with the occupancy being ''P''<sub>''α''</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;1&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;exp(&minus;''μα''), where ''μ'' is the density.<ref>Wright, D.H. 1991. Correlations between incidence and abundance are expected by chance. Journal of Biogeography, 18: 463–466.[https://www.jstor.org/stable/2845487]</ref> Clearly, P<sub>α</sub> in this Poisson model for randomly distributed individuals is also the SPO. Other probability distributions, such as the [[negative binomial distribution]], can also be applied for describing the SPO and the occupancy-abundance relationship for non-randomly distributed individuals.<ref>He, F., Gaston, K.J. 2000. Estimating species abundance from occurrence. American Naturalist, 156: 553–559.[https://www.jstor.org/stable/3079057]</ref>

Other occupancy-abundance models that can be used to describe the SPO includes Nachman's exponential model,<ref>Nachman, G. 1981. A mathematical model of the functional relationship between density and spatial distribution of a population. Journal of Animal Ecology, 50: 453–460.[https://www.jstor.org/stable/4066]</ref> Hanski and Gyllenberg's [[metapopulation]] model,<ref>Hanski, I., Gyllenberg, M. 1997. Uniting two general patterns in the distribution of species. Science, 284: 334–336.[http://www.sciencemag.org/cgi/content/abstract/275/5298/397]</ref> He and Gaston's<ref>He, F., Gaston, K.J. 2003. Occupancy, spatial variance, and the abundance of species. American Naturalist, 162: 366–375.[https://www.jstor.org/stable/3473189]</ref> improved negative binomial model by applying [[Taylor's law|Taylor's power law]] between the mean and variance of species distribution,<ref>Taylor, L.R. 1961. Aggregation, variance and the mean. Nature, 189: 732–735.[http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v189/n4766/abs/189732a0.html]</ref> and Hui and McGeoch's droopy-tail percolation model.<ref>Hui, C., McGeoch, MA. 2007. Capturing the "droopy tail" in the occupancy-abundance relationship. Ecoscience, 14: 103–108.[http://www.bioone.org/doi/abs/10.2980/1195-6860%282007%2914%5B103%3ACTDITO%5D2.0.CO%3B2?journalCode=ecos]</ref> One important application of the SPO in ecology is to estimate [[species abundance]] based on presence-absence data, or occupancy alone.<ref>Hartley, S., Kunin, WE. 2003. Scale dependence of rarity, extinction risk, and conservation priority. Conservation Biology, 17: 1559&ndash;1570.</ref> This is appealing because obtaining presence-absence data is often cost-efficient. Using a dipswitch test consisting of 5 subtests and 15 criteria, [[Cang Hui|Hui]] et al.<ref>Hui, C., McGeoch, M.A., Reyers, B., le Roux, P.C., Greve, M., Chown, S.L. 2009. Extrapolating population size from the occupancy-abundance relationship and the scaling pattern of occupancy. Ecological Applications, 19: 2038–2048.[http://www.esajournals.org/doi/abs/10.1890/08-2236.1]</ref> confirmed that using the SPO is robust and reliable for assemblage-scale regional [[abundance estimation]]. The other application of SPOs includes trends identification in populations, which is extremely valuable for [[biodiversity]] [[Conservation biology|conservation]].<ref>Wilson, RJ., Thomas, CD., Fox, R., Roy, RD., Kunin, WE. 2004. Spatial patterns in species distributions reveals biodiversity change. Nature, 432: 393–396.[http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v432/n7015/abs/nature03031.html]</ref>

== Explanation ==

Models providing explanations to the observed scaling pattern of occupancy include the [[fractal]] model, the cross-scale model and the Bayesian estimation model. The fractal model can be configured by dividing the landscape into quadrats of different sizes,<ref>Hasting, H.M. & Sugihara, G. (1993) Fractals: a User's Guide for the Natural Sciences. Oxford University Press.</ref><ref>Kunin, WE. 1998. Extrapolating species abundance across spatial scales. Science, 281: 1513&ndash;1515.</ref> or bisecting into grids with special width-to-length ratio (2:1),<ref>Harte, J., Kinzig, A.P. & Green, J. (1999) Self-similarity in the distribution and abundance of species. Science 294, 334–336.[http://www.sciencemag.org/cgi/content/full/284/5412/334]</ref><ref>Hui, C. & McGeoch, M.A. (2007) A self-similarity model for occupancy frequency distributions. Theoretical Population Biology 71: 61–70.[https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.tpb.2006.07.007]</ref> and yields the following SPO:

: <math>P_a=P_0 a^{D/2-1} \, </math>

where ''D'' is the box-counting [[fractal dimension]]. If during each step a quadrat is divided into ''q'' sub-quadrats, we will find a constant portion (''f'') of sub-quadrats is also present in the fractal model, i.e. ''D''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2(1&nbsp;+&nbsp;log&nbsp;''&fnof;''/log&nbsp;''q''). Since this assumption that ''f'' is scale independent is not always the case in nature,<ref>Hui, C. & McGeoch, M.A. (2007) Modeling species distributions by breaking the assumption of self-similarity. Oikos 116: 2097–2107.[https://dx.doi.org/10.1111/j.2007.0030-1299.16149.x]</ref> a more general form of ''&fnof;'' can be assumed, ''&fnof;''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''q''<sup>&minus;''λ''</sup> (''λ'' is a constant), which yields the cross-scale model:<ref>Lennon, J.J., Kunin, W.E., Hartley, S. & Gaston, K.J. (2007) Species distribution patterns, diversity scaling and testing for fractals in southern African birds. In: Scaling Biology (D. Storch, P.A. Marquet & J.H. Brown, eds.), pp. 51&ndash;76. Cambridge University Press.</ref>

: <math>P_{a_j}=f_0 f_1 \cdots  f_j. \, </math>

The Bayesian estimation model follows a different way of thinking. Instead of providing the best-fit model as above, the occupancy at different scales can be estimated by Bayesian rule based on not only the occupancy but also the spatial [[autocorrelation]] at one specific scale. For the Bayesian estimation model, [[Cang Hui|Hui]] et al.<ref>Hui, C., McGeoch, M.A. & Warren, M. (2006) A spatially explicitly approach to estimating species occupancy and spatial correlation. Journal of Animal Ecology 75: 140–147.[https://dx.doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2656.2005.01029.x]</ref> provide the following formula to describe the SPO and join-count statistics of spatial autocorrelation:

: <math>p\,{(4a)_+}=1 - \frac{{\Omega }^4}{\mho }</math>

: <math>q\,{(4a)_{+/+}}=\frac{{\Omega }^{10} - 
    2\,{\Omega }^4\,
     {\mho }^2 + {\mho }^3}
    {{\mho }^2\,
    \left( -{\Omega }^4 + 
      \mho  \right) }</math>

where Ω&nbsp;=&nbsp;''p''(''a'')<sub>0</sub>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''q''(''a'')<sub>0/+</sub>''p''(''a'')<sub>+</sub> and <math>\mho</math>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''p''(''a'')<sub>0</sub>(1&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''p''(''a'')<sub>+</sub><sup>2</sup>(2''q''(''a'')<sub>+/+</sub>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;3)&nbsp;+&nbsp;p(a)<sub>+</sub>(''q''(''a'')<sub>+/+</sub><sup>2</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;3)). ''p''(''a'')<sub>+</sub> is occupancy; ''q''(''a'')<sub>+/+</sub> is the conditional probability that a randomly chosen adjacent quadrat of an occupied quadrat is also occupied. The conditional probability ''q''(''a'')<sub>0/+</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;1&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''q''(''a'')<sub>+/+</sub> is the absence probability in a quadrate adjacent to an occupied one; ''a'' and 4''a'' are the grains. The R-code of the Bayesian estimation model has been provided elsewhere. The key point of the Bayesian estimation model is that the scaling pattern of species distribution, measured by occupancy and spatial pattern, can be extrapolated across scales. Later on, [[Cang Hui|Hui]]<ref>Hui, C. (2009) On the scaling patterns of species spatial distribution and association. Journal of Theoretical Biology 261: 481–487.[https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.jtbi.2009.08.015]</ref> provides the Bayesian estimation model for continuously changing scales:

: <math>P_a = 1-b c^{2a^{1/2}} h^a \, </math>

where ''b'', ''c'', and ''h'' are constants.  This SPO becomes the Poisson model when ''b''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''c''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1. In the same paper, the scaling pattern of join-count spatial autocorrelation and multi-species association (or [[co-occurrence]]) were also provided by the Bayesian model, suggesting that "''the Bayesian model can grasp the statistical essence of species scaling patterns.''"

== Implications for biological conservation ==

The probability of species extinction and [[ecosystem collapse]] increases rapidly as range size declines. In [[risk assessment]] protocols such as the [[IUCN Red List]] of Species or the [[IUCN Red List of Ecosystems]], '''area of occupancy (AOO)''' is used as a standardized, complementary and widely applicable measure of risk spreading against spatially explicit threats.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Murray|first1=Nicholas J.|last2=Keith|first2=David A.|last3=Bland|first3=Lucie M.|last4=Nicholson|first4=Emily|last5=Regan|first5=Tracey J.|last6=Rodríguez6,7,8|first6=Jon Paul|last7=Bedward|first7=Michael|title=The use of range size to assess risks to biodiversity from stochastic threats|journal=Diversity and Distributions|volume=23|issue=5|date=2017|pages=474–483|doi=10.1111/ddi.12533|doi-access=free|bibcode=2017DivDi..23..474M |hdl=10536/DRO/DU:30091065|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Murray|first1=Nicholas|title=Global 10 x 10-km grids suitable for use in IUCN Red List of Ecosystems assessments (vector and raster format)|journal=Figshare|date=2017|doi=10.6084/m9.figshare.4653439.v1}}</ref>
